nonchalant

non-shuh-LAHNT · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Nonchalant is casually calm and relaxed; unconcerned.

The intern's nonchalant response to spilling coffee on the CEO's laptop -- a shrug and a quick 'oops' -- stunned the whole office.

Example

Even after losing the championship game in the final second, the team captain gave a nonchalant wave to the cameras, as if the outcome barely mattered to him.

Nonchalant describes a casual, unbothered attitude -- the captain isn't hiding devastation, he genuinely seems unconcerned, at least on the surface.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

indifferent: Indifferent means truly having no interest or concern -- the feeling underneath is missing. Nonchalant is about the surface: a nonchalant person looks casually unconcerned but may care a great deal underneath. Indifference is real not-caring; nonchalance can be an act.

offhand: Offhand describes something done or said casually, without much thought or preparation -- an offhand remark is tossed out in passing. Nonchalant describes a whole unbothered attitude, which can be carefully kept up. You can rehearse looking nonchalant; an offhand comment is by definition unrehearsed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

anxious: worried or nervous

flustered: agitated and confused

Where it sits · how little the person cares

relaxed → nonchalant → apathetic

relaxed vs. nonchalant: Relaxed is milder than nonchalant -- relaxed is simple ease when nothing much is at stake, while a nonchalant person acts casually unconcerned about something that actually matters.

apathetic vs. nonchalant: Apathetic is deeper than nonchalant -- a nonchalant person plays it cool on the surface and may still care underneath, while an apathetic person has genuinely stopped caring about the thing at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — non-: not (Latin)

root — chal-: to care, to be concerned (literally, 'to be warm about') (French chaloir, from Latin calere)

suffix — -ant: being in a state of (adjective-forming) (Latin -ans)

Put it together: Nonchalant comes from non- ('not') + chaloir ('to care, to matter,' from Latin calere, 'to be warm') + -ant -- literally 'not being warmed up about' something, i.e., unconcerned.

Use the root in a new word: calorie: The recipe card listed exactly two hundred calories per serving.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Nonchalant describes a general attitude of not caring or not being bothered, often about something that hasn't necessarily caused any real disturbance. That's different from unperturbed, which specifically describes staying calm despite something that would normally cause distress or agitation -- you can be nonchalant about a minor inconvenience without ever having faced a real crisis to stay unperturbed through.
